From temperature data published in 'Water Quality Investations for the Howard Creek Basin" (June 1975), it appears that the natural temperature of the basin rarely approaches this stress temperature. The biological benefit of increasing flow, but at the same time increasing temperature above natural conditions, would seem of little value. If the flow were augmented only to the highest temperature observed at this stream section, the amount of augmentation would be proportionately less. Further, the South Carolina water laws will not allow temperature increases in excess of 3° F. for trout waters. With these constraints it does not appear that meaningful thow augmentation would be feasible for summer periods nor can this be considered mitigation for negative impacts.

The use of flow augmentation to flush sediment is suggested in several places but recent sediment studies in the basin indicate that extremely high (flood) flows are necessary to effectively suspend and transport sediment.
